atoms.text: The simulated resort for the dead: elderly people can visit and eventually upload to a virtual town, so heaven is a subscription service.
The time-shifting visitor: characters meet in different decades within the simulation, so the same place hosts multiple eras at once.
The dying woman who refuses upload: one partner wants eternity and the other wants to end, so love is tested by divergent afterlives.
The choice of permanence: uploading means leaving the physical world, so immortality is framed as a decision about what counts as living.
The body in the hospital: the elderly self and the young avatar coexist, so identity spans two bodies and two times.
The closeted past: one character was paralyzed after her parents rejected her coming out, so the simulation offers a second adolescence.
The trial visit: the living can visit the simulation before death, so the boundary between life and afterlife is a turnstile.
The engagement ring: a character claims to be engaged, so commitment is complicated by a past she cannot leave.
Nostalgia as a trap: the simulation is built from a preferred decade, so paradise is also a loop.
The husband who waits outside: a living spouse is left behind by the upload, so eternity creates a new kind of widowhood.
The car crash that caused paralysis: a single accident defines a life and becomes the reason to escape into simulation.
The beach town: the simulated setting is a permanent vacation, so pleasure without change becomes its own kind of death.
The ethics of euthanasia for upload: ending a body to preserve a mind, so the story asks where the person really lives.
The different decades: the same character appears in several eras, so the simulation is a wardrobe of times.
The reveal of the simulation: the audience learns the town is virtual midway, so the earlier romance is retroactively recontextualized.
Love as the argument for immortality: the couple's bond is the only thing that makes eternity desirable, so the story grounds metaphysics in romance.
